WHAT COPYRIGHT DOES NOT PROTECT — IDEAS, FACTS, MERGER, AND SCENES A FAIRE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

PURPOSE OF THIS UNPROTECTABLE ELEMENTS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the boundaries that federal copyright law places on what a copyright covers: the statutory exclusion of ideas, procedures, processes, systems, methods of operation, concepts, principles, and discoveries in 17 U.S.C. section 102(b); the limitation of a compilation or derivative work copyright to the material the later author contributed, in 17 U.S.C. section 103(b); the distinction drawn in Baker v. Selden between a book that explains an art and the art it explains; the holdings of Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co. that originality is the constitutional prerequisite to copyright, that facts are discovered rather than created and so are not copyrightable, and that the copyright in a factual compilation is accordingly thin; the merger and scenes a faire doctrines as stated by the Ninth Circuit in Ets-Hokin v. Skyy Spirits, Inc.; the treatment of ideas and standard elements, and of combinations of unprotectable elements, in Satava v. Lowry; the relationship in Mattel, Inc. v. MGA Entertainment, Inc. between the range of possible expression and whether infringement requires substantial similarity or virtual identity; and the Ninth Circuit's en banc treatment in Skidmore v. Led Zeppelin of common building blocks and of selection-and-arrangement claims. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the following work: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., and the following elements or features of that work: The order of the species entries, the range-map shading scheme, and the photographs of bees on flowers. This Information Sheet describes what the cited statutes and decisions say; it does not itself determine whether any particular element of any particular work is protected, unprotected, original, merged, standard, or infringed, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE STATUTORY LINE: 17 U.S.C. § 102(A) AND § 102(B)
Section 102 of the Copyright Act states both what copyright protects and what it does not. Subsection (a) provides that copyright protection subsists in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated either directly or with the aid of a machine or device, and it lists eight categories of works of authorship: literary works; musical works, including any accompanying words; dramatic works, including any accompanying music; pantomimes and choreographic works; pictorial, graphic, and sculptural works; motion pictures and other audiovisual works; sound recordings; and architectural works. Subsection (b), added in the 1976 general revision, states the exclusion: in no case does copyright protection for an original work of authorship extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in that work. The exclusion is phrased in terms of the categories of subject matter that fall outside copyright, not in terms of a defense, and it applies regardless of how the idea or method is expressed in the work.

COMPILATIONS AND DERIVATIVE WORKS: 17 U.S.C. § 103(B)
Section 103 addresses works that are built out of preexisting material. Subsection (a) provides that the subject matter of copyright specified by section 102 includes compilations and derivative works, but that protection for a work employing preexisting material in which copyright subsists does not extend to any part of the work in which that material has been used unlawfully. Subsection (b) states the limit that matters when the preexisting material is unprotected in the first place: the copyright in a compilation or derivative work extends only to the material contributed by the author of that work, as distinguished from the preexisting material employed in it, and does not imply any exclusive right in the preexisting material. The subsection adds that the copyright in such a work is independent of, and does not affect or enlarge the scope, duration, ownership, or subsistence of, any copyright protection in the preexisting material. A compilation of unprotected facts or of public domain elements is therefore capable of being copyrighted as a compilation while the underlying facts and elements themselves remain outside the copyright.

THE BOOK AND THE ART IT EXPLAINS ARE DIFFERENT THINGS (BAKER V. SELDEN)
Baker v. Selden is the decision from which the American idea/expression distinction descends. Charles Selden had copyrighted books explaining a system of bookkeeping, illustrated with ruled lines and blank columns with headings; the defendant used a similar arrangement of columns and headings. The Supreme Court held that a book explaining an art may be copyrighted as a book, but that the copyright in the book gives no exclusive right in the art the book describes. The Court drew a clear distinction between the book, as such, and the art which it is intended to illustrate, and applied the same distinction to treatises on medicines, ploughs, watches, churns, dyeing, and perspective drawing: no one would contend that the copyright of the treatise would give the exclusive right to the art or manufacture described in it. The Court located the reason in the difference between the two federal regimes: an exclusive right in an art or manufacture may be secured only by a patent, after examination for novelty, while the validity of the copyright in a book does not depend on the novelty of what the book describes. To give the author of a book an exclusive property in the art described in it, where no examination of novelty had ever been officially made, would in the Court's words be a surprise and a fraud upon the public.

METHODS AND DIAGRAMS NECESSARY TO USE AN ART ARE GIVEN TO THE PUBLIC (BAKER V. SELDEN)
Baker v. Selden also supplies the reasoning later courts describe as the merger principle. The Court explained that the very object of publishing a book on science or the useful arts is to communicate to the world the useful knowledge which it contains, and that this object would be frustrated if the knowledge could not be used without incurring the guilt of piracy of the book. It followed, the Court said, that where the art a book teaches cannot be used without employing the methods and diagrams used to illustrate the book, or ones similar to them, those methods and diagrams are to be considered necessary incidents to the art and given to the public along with it -- not given for the purpose of publication in other works explaining the art, but for the purpose of practical application. Applying that reasoning, the Court held that any person may practise and use the art itself which the author has described and illustrated, that the copyright of a book on bookkeeping cannot secure the exclusive right to make, sell, and use account books prepared on the plan the book sets out, and that blank account books are not the subject of copyright.

ORIGINALITY IS THE PREREQUISITE, AND IT IS NOT NOVELTY (FEIST PUBLICATIONS)
In Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., the Supreme Court considered whether a telephone company's white pages listings could be copyrighted, and in doing so restated the basic requirement for copyright in any work. The Court described the case as concerning the interaction of two well-established propositions: that facts are not copyrightable, and that compilations of facts generally are. The key to the tension, the Court said, lies in understanding why facts are not copyrightable, and that key is originality. Original, as the term is used in copyright, means only that the work was independently created by the author, as opposed to copied from other works, and that it possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity. The Court emphasized that the required level of creativity is extremely low and that even a slight amount will suffice, and that originality does not signify novelty: a work may be original even though it closely resembles other works, so long as the similarity is fortuitous rather than the result of copying. The Court also held that originality is not merely a statutory requirement but a constitutional one, rooted in the terms "authors" and "writings" in Article I, section 8, clause 8 of the Constitution.

FACTS ARE DISCOVERED, NOT CREATED, AND SO ARE NOT COPYRIGHTABLE (FEIST PUBLICATIONS)
Feist explained why facts fall outside copyright even when finding them took great effort. Facts do not owe their origin to an act of authorship, the Court said; the distinction is one between creation and discovery, and the first person to find and report a particular fact has not created the fact but has merely discovered its existence. The Court gave census takers as an illustration: they do not create the population figures that emerge from their efforts, but in a sense copy those figures from the world around them, so census data are not original in the constitutional sense. The same is true, the Court said, of all facts -- scientific, historical, biographical, and news of the day. On that basis the Court rejected the "sweat of the brow" or "industrious collection" doctrine that some lower courts had used to protect factual compilations, describing its most glaring flaw as extending copyright protection beyond the compiler's original contributions of selection and arrangement to the facts themselves. In holding that the white pages listings lacked the requisite originality, the Court said its decision should not be construed as demeaning the compiler's efforts but as making clear that copyright rewards originality, not effort.

THE COPYRIGHT IN A FACTUAL COMPILATION IS THIN (FEIST PUBLICATIONS)
Feist described what remains protectable when an author assembles unprotected material. Where a compiler adds original written expression, that expression may be protected; where the compiler lets the facts speak for themselves, the only conceivable expression is the manner in which the facts have been selected and arranged, and those elements are eligible for protection if the selection and arrangement are original. But no matter how original the format, the Court said, the facts themselves do not become original through association. The consequence the Court drew is that the copyright in a factual compilation is thin: notwithstanding a valid copyright, a subsequent compiler remains free to use the facts contained in another's publication to aid in preparing a competing work, so long as the competing work does not feature the same selection and arrangement. The Court tied this result to the purpose of copyright, which is not to reward the labor of authors but to promote the progress of science and useful arts, and described the principle -- known as the idea/expression or fact/expression dichotomy -- as applying to all works of authorship, with the consequence that in a factual compilation only the compiler's selection and arrangement may be protected while the raw facts may be copied at will.

MERGER AND SCENES A FAIRE AS THE NINTH CIRCUIT STATES THEM (ETS-HOKIN V. SKYY SPIRITS)
In Ets-Hokin v. Skyy Spirits, Inc., a dispute over commercial photographs of a vodka bottle, the Ninth Circuit set out the two related doctrines that courts use to keep copyright off ideas that can be expressed in only one or a few ways. Under the merger doctrine, courts will not protect a copyrighted work from infringement if the idea underlying the copyrighted work can be expressed in only one way, lest there be a monopoly on the underlying idea; in such an instance the work's idea and expression are said to merge. Under the related doctrine of scenes a faire, courts will not protect a copyrighted work from infringement if the expression embodied in the work necessarily flows from a commonplace idea; as with merger, the rationale is that there should be no monopoly on the underlying unprotectable idea. The court noted that courts have disagreed about whether these doctrines bear on copyrightability or instead operate as defenses to infringement, and held for the Ninth Circuit that they are defenses to infringement, to be addressed in the first instance by the district court in the context of the infringement claims.

IDEAS AND STANDARD ELEMENTS BELONG TO THE PUBLIC (SATAVA V. LOWRY)
Satava v. Lowry concerned glass-in-glass sculptures of jellyfish made by two artists. The Ninth Circuit described Congress as having granted artists the exclusive right to the original expression in their works while denying them the exclusive right to ideas and standard elements, thereby preventing them from monopolizing what rightfully belongs to the public. The originality requirement, the court said, means that objective facts and ideas are not copyrightable, and expressions that are standard, stock, or common to a particular subject matter or medium are likewise not protectable. Applying that principle, the court held that no copyright protection may be afforded to the idea of producing a glass-in-glass jellyfish sculpture or to elements of expression that naturally follow from that idea: the artist could not prevent others from depicting jellyfish with tendril-like tentacles or rounded bells, because many jellyfish have those body parts; nor in bright colors, because many jellyfish are brightly colored; nor swimming vertically, because jellyfish swim vertically in nature; nor within a clear outer layer of glass, because clear glass is the most appropriate setting for an aquatic animal. Nature gives us ideas of animals in their natural surroundings, the court said, and those ideas, first expressed by nature, are the common heritage of humankind, which no artist may use copyright law to prevent others from depicting.

WHEN A COMBINATION OF UNPROTECTABLE ELEMENTS IS ITSELF PROTECTABLE (SATAVA V. LOWRY)
Satava also addressed the argument that even if each element of a work is unprotectable, the combination of those elements is protected. The Ninth Circuit accepted that a combination of unprotectable elements may qualify for copyright protection, but held that not every combination does: a combination of unprotectable elements is eligible for copyright protection only if those elements are numerous enough and their selection and arrangement original enough that their combination constitutes an original work of authorship. Applying that rule, the court held that the particular combination before it -- clear glass, an oblong shroud, bright colors, proportion, vertical orientation, and a stereotyped jellyfish form -- lacked the quantum of originality needed, because those elements are so commonplace in the medium and so typical of jellyfish physiology that protecting their combination would effectively give one artist a monopoly on lifelike glass-in-glass sculptures of single vertical jellyfish. The court did not say the artist had added nothing copyrightable: it identified distinctive curls of particular tendrils, the arrangement of certain hues, and the unique shape of the bells as original contributions, and held that the resulting copyright is thin, protecting against only virtually identical copying.

WHAT A SELECTION-AND-ARRANGEMENT CLAIM REQUIRES (SKIDMORE V. LED ZEPPELIN)
Skidmore also addressed the recurring argument that a plaintiff may assemble unprotectable elements into a combination and sue on the combination. expectedJSON.body: Feist described what remains protectable when an author assembles unprotected material. Where a compiler adds original written expression, that expression may be protected; where the compiler lets the facts speak for themselves, the only conceivable expression is the manner in which the facts have been selected and arranged, and those elements are eligible for protection if the selection and arrangement are original. But no matter how original the format, the Court said, the facts themselves do not become original through association. The consequence the Court drew is that the copyright in a factual compilation is thin: notwithstanding a valid copyright, a subsequent compiler remains free to use the facts contained in another's publication to aid in preparing a competing work, so long as the competing work does not feature the same selection and arrangement. The Court tied this result to the purpose of copyright, which is not to reward the labor of authors but to promote the progress of science and useful arts, and described the principle -- known as the idea/expression or fact/expression dichotomy -- as applying to all works of authorship, with the consequence that in a factual compilation only the compiler's selection and arrangement may be protected while the raw facts may be copied at will.

expectedJSON.body: In Ets-Hokin v. Skyy Spirits, Inc., a dispute over commercial photographs of a vodka bottle, the Ninth Circuit set out the two related doctrines that courts use to keep copyright off ideas that can be expressed in only one or a few ways. Under the merger doctrine, courts will not protect a copyrighted work from infringement if the idea underlying the copyrighted work can be expressed in only one way, lest there be a monopoly on the underlying idea; in such an instance the work's idea and expression are said to merge. Under the related doctrine of scenes a faire, courts will not protect a copyrighted work from infringement if the expression embodied in the work necessarily flows from a commonplace idea; as with merger, the rationale is that there should be no monopoly on the underlying unprotectable idea. The court noted that courts have disagreed about whether these doctrines bear on copyrightability or instead operate as defenses to infringement, and held for the Ninth Circuit that they are defenses to infringement, to be addressed in the first instance by the district court in the context of the infringement claims.

expectedJSON.body: Satava v. Lowry concerned glass-in-glass sculptures of jellyfish made by two artists. The Ninth Circuit described Congress as having granted artists the exclusive right to the original expression in their works while denying them the exclusive right to ideas and standard elements, thereby preventing them from monopolizing what rightfully belongs to the public. The originality requirement, the court said, means that objective facts and ideas are not copyrightable, and expressions that are standard, stock, or common to a particular subject matter or medium are likewise not protectable. Applying that principle, the court held that no copyright protection may be afforded to the idea of producing a glass-in-glass jellyfish sculpture or to elements of expression that naturally follow from that idea: the artist could not prevent others from depicting jellyfish with tendril-like tentacles or rounded bells, because many jellyfish have those body parts; nor in bright colors, because many jellyfish are brightly colored; nor swimming vertically, because jellyfish swim vertically in nature; nor within a clear outer layer of glass, because clear glass is the most appropriate setting for an aquatic animal. Nature gives us ideas of animals in their natural surroundings, the court said, and those ideas, first expressed by nature, are the common heritage of humankind, which no artist may use copyright law to prevent others from depicting.

expectedJSON.body: Satava also addressed the argument that even if each element of a work is unprotectable, the combination of those elements is protected. The Ninth Circuit accepted that a combination of unprotectable elements may qualify for copyright protection, but held that not every combination does: a combination of unprotectable elements is eligible for copyright protection only if those elements are numerous enough and their selection and arrangement original enough that their combination constitutes an original work of authorship. Applying that rule, the court held that the particular combination before it -- clear glass, an oblong shroud, bright colors, proportion, vertical orientation, and a stereotyped jellyfish form -- lacked the quantum of originality needed, because those elements are so commonplace in the medium and so typical of jellyfish physiology that protecting their combination would effectively give one artist a monopoly on lifelike glass-in-glass sculptures of single vertical jellyfish. The court did not say the artist had added nothing copyrightable: it identified distinctive curls of particular tendrils, the arrangement of certain hues, and the unique shape of the bells as original contributions, and held that the resulting copyright is thin, protecting against only virtually identical copying.

expectedJSON.body: In Skidmore v. Led Zeppelin, decided en banc, the Ninth Circuit applied these limits to music. Even in the face of copyright's low threshold for creativity, the court said, copyright does not protect every aspect of a work: ideas, concepts, and common elements are excluded, citing 17 U.S.C. section 102(b) and Feist. Copyright does not extend to common or trite musical elements, nor to commonplace elements that are firmly rooted in the genre's tradition. Such building blocks, the court held, belong in the public domain and cannot be exclusively appropriated by any particular author, quoting Satava for the proposition that expressions standard, stock, or common to a particular subject matter or medium are not protectable. The court explained the reason in terms of how works are made: authors borrow from predecessors' works to create new ones, so giving exclusive rights to the first author who incorporated an idea, concept, or common element would frustrate the purpose of the copyright law and curtail the creation of new works, and courts must be careful in copyright cases not to cheat the public domain.

expectedJSON.body: Skidmore also addressed the recurring argument that a plaintiff may assemble unprotectable elements into a combination and sue on the combination. Presenting a combination of unprotectable elements without explaining how those elements are particularly selected and arranged, the Ninth Circuit said, amounts to nothing more than trying to copyright commonplace elements. The word combination cannot mean any set of artistic building blocks: the court explained that only a new combination, that is a novel arrangement, and not any combination of unprotectable elements, qualifies for copyright protection. The court accordingly held that a selection and arrangement copyright is infringed only where the works share, in substantial amounts, the particular -- that is, the same -- combination of unprotectable elements, and that a plaintiff cannot establish substantial similarity by reconstituting the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements and then claiming that those same elements also appear in the defendant's work in a different aesthetic context. Because many works of art can be recast as compilations of individually unprotected parts, the court said, the contrary approach would deem vastly dissimilar compositions, novels, and paintings substantially similar merely for sharing some of the same notes, words, or colors.
